title: Melbourne: growth and services
text:
Home / Melbourne
We looked at population and facility data for 354 SA2 (Statistical Area Level 2) areas across Greater Melbourne between 2021 and 2024, drawn from ABS population estimates and the Vicmap community facilities catalogue, to see whether services are keeping pace with growth.
They’re not growing evenly. A small group of growth areas on Melbourne’s fringe — Wyndham, Melton, Casey, Hume, Whittlesea, Cardinia and Mitchell — are adding people far faster than the rest of the city. Meanwhile, established areas closer to the centre are growing slowly, if at all.

title: Melbourne: growth and services
section: Within Greater Melbourne, is everyone growing at the same speed?
text:
Within Greater Melbourne, is everyone growing at the same speed?
Melbourne isn’t growing evenly. Some areas are barely changing; others are adding people fast. This first chart shows where the fast growth is actually happening.



Not really. Each dot is an SA2 — an ABS-defined area sized to a population of roughly 3,000–25,000, used as the closest standard unit to suburb-level analysis (though SA2 boundaries don’t always match actual suburb boundaries — small suburbs are often grouped together, large ones split apart). The orange dots — growth-area SA2s — are growing noticeably faster: growth above 20% is over five times more common among them than elsewhere. Those SA2s make up 58% of the city’s fastest-growing tenth, despite being under a third of all SA2s citywide. SA2s in established areas — the rest of the city — rarely see growth above 20% at all.



Next: is that unevenness reflected in services too? →

title: Melbourne: growth and services
section: Is that unevenness reflected in services too?
text:
Is that unevenness reflected in services too?
If people are arriving unevenly, are services arriving with them? Here’s what happened to mapped facilities in the same places, over the same years.



73% of SA2s in the fastest-growing quarter saw facility provision fall behind population growth between 2021 and 2024 (a median drop of 0.10 facilities per 1,000 residents) — while slower-growing areas mostly kept pace.



← Back Next: does the pattern hold across the whole city? →

title: Melbourne: growth and services
section: Does the pattern hold across the whole city?
text:
Does the pattern hold across the whole city?
So far, that’s two snapshots — not yet a trend.



Yes — the relationship runs downhill across the whole city. Each extra 10 percentage points of population growth is associated with about 0.3 fewer mapped facilities per 1,000 residents, on average (a statistically significant trend, p < 0.001). Areas near 0% growth cluster around 2.5–3.5 facilities per 1,000; by 50%+ growth, most sit below 1.5.



← Back Next: do high-growth areas end up with fewer services? →

title: Melbourne: growth and services
section: Do high-growth areas end up with fewer services?
text:
Do high-growth areas end up with fewer services?
Put growth and facilities side by side, area by area, and a shape emerges — one that lines up closely with where the growth-area SA2s actually are.



Across Greater Melbourne, the median is about 2.3 facilities per 1,000 residents. Most SA2s grow modestly and sit close to that median. However, among the smaller number of areas growing faster than 25%, we’re seeing a gap: established areas’ facility ratio roughly plateaus (only a few established areas grow faster than about 40%). Meanwhile, growth areas keep going all the way into hyper-growth, but their facility ratio drops toward 0.4–0.5 per 1,000 despite 100%+ growth.

title: Melbourne: growth and services
section: How much of Melbourne’s growth is happening in each council?
text:
How much of Melbourne’s growth is happening in each council?
Zooming out from SA2s to whole councils: watch each council’s population change from 2010 to 2024. Use play/pause or the scrubber below the chart.






By 2024, Melbourne’s five most populous councils are exactly its five largest growth-area councils — Casey, Wyndham, Hume, Whittlesea and Melton — ahead of every established council, including Monash (Greater Melbourne’s largest established council). None of them started there: watch the race to see how recently that changed.
Colour and position mean different things here: colour is a fixed category (growth area or established, per the Victorian Government’s own designation — see below), while position is purely current population rank. The two don’t always agree — Mitchell is officially a growth area but is currently the third-smallest council in Melbourne (28,415 people, 2024), so you’ll see it coloured orange near the bottom of the chart rather than near the top.

Which services are falling behind fastest in Whittlesea?



Recreation facilities are furthest behind in Whittlesea, growing less than 1% (233 to 235) against 9% population growth. Health also lagged (+3%) and community grew modestly behind pace (+7%). Education outpaced population growth (+19%).

Suburban Futures

Melbourne has grown fast over the last decade. Have the services meant to support it kept pace? Explore where that’s true across the city — and where it isn’t. We’ll start with the citywide picture, then narrow in on a council and its stories.







































people mapped facilities


In many growth-front councils, population fills in faster than the facilities mapped to serve it. Each story shows the real numbers for one place.





As Melbourne grows, are the services meant to support it keeping up — everywhere?


Growth-area councils have far more suburbs in hyper-growth than the rest of the city — and facility supply isn’t keeping pace with that growth on average.

Community facilities have stalled in Mitchell — 10 in both 2021 and 2024 — while population grew 24%, the fastest of any growth-area council. Recreation also lagged (+13%) and education grew modestly behind pace (+19%). Mitchell has no mapped health facilities at all — zero in both 2021 and 2024 — so health isn’t shown on this chart.

title: Wyndham stories
section: Is Wyndham’s growth matched by its facilities — everywhere, or just in parts?
text:
Is Wyndham’s growth matched by its facilities — everywhere, or just in parts?
In this analysis, Wyndham’s SA2s split into three groups: established suburbs (Wyndham’s older, already-built-out areas — Hoppers Crossing and Werribee East), growth corridors (the newest greenfield fronts driving most of Wyndham’s population growth — Tarneit, Truganina, Wyndham Vale, Manor Lakes and Point Cook), and mixed areas — a small group of SA2s where substantial industrial, rural, or defence land sits alongside residential development, making them harder to compare directly to the other two. The chart below shows where each group sits on facilities versus growth.






While Wyndham’s overall facility growth has kept pace with its population growth at 17.2%, that number hides a real split within the council. A 2024 snapshot shows established parts of Wyndham had 2.76 mapped facilities per 1,000 residents — new growth areas had only 1.72. And those new growth areas are home to about two-thirds of Wyndham’s population.

A note on point size: it’s set to 2024 population rather than the 2021–2024 growth figure on the x-axis because it’s paired with the y-axis instead — facilities per 1,000 residents is itself calculated using 2024 population, so sizing points by that same year keeps the dot size consistent with the rate it’s plotted against.
